1:
Henry reads the speech as a model of how to draw others into a good work. David lays no tax on the assembly, because what is done in piety should be done willingly and God loves a cheerful giver, and instead offers three reasons: the chosen successor is young and needs help, the building is not for man but for the Lord, and the king has already spent himself on it. Ellicott glosses alone as of all his brothers, and refers the phrase about youth back to 1 Chronicles 22:5. He makes more of the word rendered palace. Birah belongs to the later books and elsewhere always means the fortress-palace at Susa; this is the single place in Scripture where it is used of the Temple, and its associations were well fitted to convey the magnificence the chronicler imagined. Clarke quotes the Targum in the same direction, that the palace was prepared not for the name of a son of man but for the name of the Word of the Lord God.

On the preparations Henry glosses with all my might as meaning that David made it his business, and takes it as a rule: work for God done with less brings nothing to pass. Ellicott works through the material list word by word. The Hebrew says simply the gold for the gold and the silver for the silver. Shoham, rendered onyx, is so uncertain that the Greek translators gave it as onyx, beryl, sardius, emerald and sapphire in different places. The stones to be set are strictly stones of fillings. The glistering stones and stones of divers colours are stones of puk and riqmah, puk being the pigment Eastern women used to darken brow and lash, so that a colour rather than a species seems meant; riqmah covers veined or variegated marble, or tesselated work.

The last item draws two witnesses the same way. Ellicott notes that shayish is read nowhere else and means white marble, that the Greek and Latin make it Parian and the Targum simply marbles. Clarke prefers Parian outright: Paros among the Cyclade islands yielded the whitest and finest marble, the stone of most great works of antiquity, and Josephus describes the temple as built of large polished blocks of it.

What the king gave out of his own estate is stated in talents, and nobody agrees what that came to. Gill passes on two reckonings, thirty-six million six hundred and sixty thousand gold ducats after Scheuchzer, or thirteen and a half million pounds after Brerewood. Delitzsch arrives near the second, about thirteen and a half million pounds, but halves it to six and three quarters if the royal shekel is the standard, and treats the silver the same way. Ellicott puts the gold at eighteen million sterling and the silver at two million eight hundred thousand. He adds that the Syriac and Arabic read a thousand thousand talents of gold and twice that of silver. On the metal itself Wesley says only that Ophir gold is the best and purest; Delitzsch agrees, matching it against the refined silver; Ellicott alone locates the place, at Abhira near the mouth of the Indus.

Where it was to go is disputed less. Delitzsch takes the overlaying as gold and silver leaf on inner walls, covering the holy place, the most holy, the porch and the upper chambers, and probably only the inner faces of the side buildings; Wesley divides it, gold for the temple and silver beaten into plates for the adjoining rooms; Ellicott notes the verb means strictly to besmear. The closing appeal is idiomatic, and Clarke, Delitzsch and Ellicott all render it literally as filling the hand for the Lord. Henry and Wesley take the same phrase devotionally: whoever engages in this service will find his hands full, for there is work in it for the whole man.
6:
Ellicott begins with a point of translation that flattens the list. Chief, princes, captains and rulers all render one Hebrew word, so the verse names one class described four ways, plus a group standing slightly apart, the stewards of the royal estates. Delitzsch identifies those last with the officials catalogued earlier in the book, the overseers of the king's property and cattle, and both take the particle before them as inclusive. Gill simply calls the first group the princes of the twelve tribes.

What they gave is stated in talents, and the conversions diverge as widely as they did over the royal gift. Clarke works from a talent of five thousand and seventy-five pounds odd and reaches over twenty-five million sterling for the five thousand talents of gold, adding that on Dr Prideaux's higher estimate the figure would be considerably greater. Ellicott puts the same quantity at between thirty and forty millions and marks the sum with an exclamation. Delitzsch gives twenty-two and a half millions, or eleven and a half on the royal standard. For the silver Clarke computes rather over three and a half million, Ellicott about four, and Ellicott notes that Schrader, arguing from Assyrian data, lowers it to three and three quarters. Clarke alone converts the base metals, turning eighteen thousand talents of brass into something past a thousand tons and a hundred thousand talents of iron into some five thousand seven hundred; Ellicott observes only that bronze and iron were worth far more then than now.

The ten thousand drams occasion the sharpest philology in the chapter, and here the witnesses agree. Delitzsch denies that the Hebrew word answers to the Greek drachma or the Arabic dirhem and derives it instead from the daric, pointing to the Syriac rendering at Ezra 8:27 and citing the numismatic literature for surviving specimens; he values it at about twenty-two shillings and sixpence. Ellicott agrees, naming Darius son of Hystaspes as the first to strike it, noting that it stayed current in Western Asia long after Persia fell, that the word recurs in Scripture only at that one place in Ezra, and that the Talmud knows it too. Clarke values it a little lower, at about twenty shillings. Ellicott then draws a conclusion the others do not: since no real coins are named anywhere in Scripture before the exile, the chronicler or his source must have substituted a currency familiar to his own readers for whatever the older record said.

The gift of jewels is handled briefly. Ellicott points out that the Hebrew uses the article where English needs a relative, and that the stones went to the temple treasure under the charge of Jehiel, whose Gershonite house had that office; he compares the like offering of the princes in Exodus. Gill only cross-refers to the list already given.

On the gladness that followed, the witnesses divide the credit. Henry insists that although the people were persuaded into it they gave willingly and with a perfect heart, which is said by one who knew their hearts, and that they gave like princes of Israel. He reads the rejoicing two ways, either the givers pleased at the chance to honour God and at the prospect of the work finished, or the commons pleased with rulers so forward in it. Wesley finds three things in the same joy, the grace of God working in them, a token of divine favour toward them, and a pledge that the long-desired building would now go up quickly. Both then turn to the old king's own joy, which Henry traces to seeing the fruit of his psalms and other helps to devotion, and to knowing that his successor would be surrounded by such men; it is a great reviving, as Wesley puts it, for good men leaving the world to see those they leave behind zealous for it.
10:
Delitzsch frames the prayer by its occasion. Since the decree had given the building not to the man of war but to the peace-king, the old servant of the Lord had done what he could to prepare for it, and now found the chiefs of the nation willing to carry it through; in that willingness he saw a particular proof of divine favour, and closes the last parliament of his reign by thanking God before the whole assembly. Henry expects the prayer from what precedes, since a man who rejoices as this one did will make his rejoicing the matter of his thanksgiving, and notes that the blessing was public and not private. Both he and Wesley draw the same lesson from the king's age: it becomes the old and dying to have their hearts enlarged in praise, and the nearer one comes to the world of everlasting praise the more its language should be spoken now. Gill adds the theology under it: David ascribed to God the ability and the willingness alike, knowing who works in men both to will and to do.

Ellicott sets the piece in literary history. The spirit that once found its outlet in the odes of psalmists and the trumpet-tones of prophets ran, in later days when psalmody had weakened and prophecy died, into impassioned prayer, and he is careful to say that the chronicler, or more likely his source, puts this utterance into the aged king's mouth. On the opening address he insists the words join as Israel our father and not as Jehovah our father, adding that though the divine fatherhood is affirmed here and there by the prophets it never became a governing idea within Old Testament limits. The closing phrase he renders from eternity even unto eternity, and compares the doxologies that close two books of the Psalter.

Over the great ascription Henry and Ellicott agree by different routes. Henry hears the stress on the definite article: not that God is great and powerful and glorious, but that his is the greatness, the power, the glory, which he holds in and of himself while every creature holds them derivatively. Ellicott puts it as self-effacement, David arrogating nothing and referring the scale of his kingdom, the prowess of his soldiers and the splendour of his throne to their owner. He then unpicks the vocabulary: the word for greatness is late, the word for power means properly manly strength and so valour, the word rendered victory means glory or splendour and gets its English sense from the Syriac and the old versions, and the clause about being exalted as head is awkward enough that Ewald treats the participle as an Aramaized infinitive. He suspects a pronoun has dropped out in two places.

Clarke contributes the Targum, which turns the verse into a recital of history: the world created by that power, the fathers led out of Egypt, the passage of the Red Sea, the appearing on Sinai with troops of angels, the victories over Amalek and over Sihon and Og, the sun halted at Gibeon and the moon in Ajalon, and a kingdom in the firmament exalted over angels and over all earthly rulers.

Gill and Ellicott meet on the twelfth verse. Gill observes that whatever men have of wealth or standing comes not from merit, diligence or good management but from providence, remarking that even the heathen made their gods the givers of riches; Ellicott reads it literally as from before thee, and notes that the two English words power and might translate each other's Hebrew from verse to verse. On the thanksgiving that closes the paragraph both Delitzsch and Ellicott point to the participles, which make it not one act of thanks but a praise continually rising afresh, and Ellicott adds that the noun for thanking, and the phrase the name of thy glory, occur nowhere else.
14:
The turn from praise to self-abasement is the point every witness marks. Henry notices how odd it looks in context: the speaker is at the height of his standing, presiding over a great assembly, naming his heir and making a magnificent gift, and in that posture calls himself and the most honourable nation then alive unworthy of notice. Gill puts the same thought as dust and ashes receiving an honour it has no claim to, and Wesley reads the wonder as double, that God should give both the wealth to offer and the willing mind to offer it, each of them a fruit of grace. Delitzsch fixes the grammar, taking the idiom as holding strength together, a phrase confined to Chronicles and Daniel; Ellicott counts the same nine occurrences.

On the ground of the humility all four speak at once. Delitzsch explains the strangers and sojourners by tenure: the land was held in usufruct only, and so is everything a man has, a loan committed rather than a possession. Wesley says it in the language of estate: they were not proprietors but tenants, strangers once even before men and no better before God now. Clarke glosses sojourners as lodging for a night in another man's house, and finds in the closing clause not merely impermanence but the absence of any expectation of exemption from the changes their fathers met; he adds the Targum, which makes the days a bird's shadow flying through the air of heaven, with no hope to any man of living for ever. Ellicott presses the same word to mean no hope and no assured future, and asks what the plaintive turn is for, answering that it emphasises what precedes: creatures of a day can hold nothing absolutely.

Henry turns the brevity into an argument against merit. A service confined to so narrow a span can pretend to earn nothing, and he notes that the speaker puts himself not merely among those who must own their days a shadow but at the front of them, though his own life had as much substance in it as most. Wesley draws the practical inference, that men give God only what they must shortly leave and cannot keep, so that his accepting such offerings is itself a favour.

The refrain about giving back what was received is where Clarke and Wesley find the doctrine. Clarke quotes the Targum again, that from the divine presence all good comes and of the blessings of those hands the offering is made; Wesley extends it beyond money to every good thought, desire and work. Henry attaches the caution he thinks the princes needed, that none of them should reckon they had merited anything, since what they returned was a small part of what they had received. Gill pauses over the scale and reports two computations, Jacob Leon reckoning the gold at tens of thousands of tons and the silver at nearly as much, Witsius bringing both together at something over twenty thousand tons of gold, doubled again if these were sanctuary talents.

The prayer closes on the heart, and the witnesses stay close together. Delitzsch and Ellicott both take the appeal to the searcher of hearts as warrant for the claim to have given without grudging, Ellicott spelling out the logic: the motive was not self-interest but glory, so the thanksgiving can be joyful. Both render the petition for the people as asking that the present frame of mind be given permanence and the heart directed rather than merely prepared; Wesley prefers confirm, since what grace began grace must carry on, and Clarke says the dispositions came from God and must be sustained by the same means. For the heir the request is an undivided heart, which Delitzsch and Ellicott both connect to keeping the commandments and completing the building already provided for.
20:
Ellicott begins by removing a false note of time: the now that opens the summons is not temporal but a particle of entreaty, bless ye, I pray. He suspects the response used a set form, like the doxologies that close the books of the Psalter, and traces the two gestures carefully, the first a bowing which the Greek renders sometimes as bending the knee and usually as stooping, the second a full prostration; the pair, he observes, is almost never separated in Hebrew. Delitzsch notes the same fixed collocation. The awkward object of that worship is faced by everyone. Clarke distinguishes the reverence given to God as supreme Ruler from that given to the king as his deputy, Wesley calls the one religious and the other civil, and Ellicott grounds the honour in representation, the throne being held for another. Henry adds the caution that whoever speaks for a congregation, only those share the benefit who join him, and that joining is done less by bowing the head than by lifting the soul.

The feast follows on the next day, a phrase Ellicott notes occurs here only. Delitzsch sets out the arithmetic of it: a thousand bullocks, a thousand rams and a thousand lambs as burnt offering, with drink offerings to match, and then thank offerings in quantity, so that everyone present could share the meal. Both he and Ellicott point out that the word for sacrifices is general at the start of the verse and narrowed by the contrast later, where it must mean the offerings from which joyous meals were made. Clarke reports the Targum putting the libations at a thousand as well, equalling the victims, and describes the second class as peace offerings whose flesh the people ate. Gill locates the eating and drinking before the ark, in the tent that had been pitched for it.

That Solomon was made king a second time sends every witness back to the hurried first occasion. Clarke recalls it as done in haste and without pomp while Adonijah was reaching for the throne, and holds that this second ceremony took place with full rites and sacrifices once everything was quiet, the father being by then probably dead. Wesley agrees about the emergency of the first. Delitzsch and Ellicott both cross-refer to the brief earlier notice, and both take the phrase to Jehovah as meaning in accordance with his will rather than in his presence, since the preposition will not carry the latter. Clarke states the principle bluntly, that God never surrendered his own right to be king in Israel and those called kings were only his lieutenants.

The anointing of Zadok in the same breath divides them. Delitzsch infers that the high priesthood came to him with the consent of the estates of the kingdom. Ellicott calls the notice remarkable and peculiar to this book, finds in it a vivid illustration of the almost sovereign dignity of the office, and takes it as showing that the removal of Abiathar was already in the old king's mind. Wesley denies that the ceremony made Zadok high priest at all: a high priest might have a deputy to officiate, and this act settled only the reversion after Abiathar's death, exactly as anointing Solomon gave him a right without putting him in possession, which is why Abiathar went on exercising the office until he was thrust out.

Henry takes the throne itself as the point to end on. What Solomon sat upon is called the throne of the Lord, and his kingdom is read as a type of the Messiah's, whose throne is that same throne.
23:
Why the seat is called the throne of the Lord draws the fullest answer from Henry. Not the throne prepared in the heavens, but the throne of Israel, so named because God was king of that nation in a peculiar manner, having both founded the throne and filled it by direct appointment; their civil laws were divine, and Urim and prophets served their princes as a privy council. Wesley says the same more briefly, and Gill puts it as vicegerency, the occupant ruling a people not his own. Ellicott and Delitzsch content themselves with cross-referring to the earlier statement of the idea, Delitzsch adding that the note of prosperity answers exactly to the hope the father had expressed for his son.

Both of those two also explain why these verses sit where they do. Ellicott warns against reading an abdication into the phrase about reigning instead of his father: the paragraph anticipates the reign that follows, and stands here because it reports the immediate sequel of the coronation and shows the old king's last wishes coming true. Delitzsch says the same from the other side, that a history of David's reign is not complete without them, since they record the fulfilment of what he had asked for the son God chose.

The act of submission is described by an idiom nobody can quite place, and the three explanations do not agree. Clarke translates it literally, they gave the hand under Solomon, and identifies it with the oath-taking ceremony of putting the hand beneath the thigh. Henry accepts that derivation and offers an alternative beside it, that the phrase may express devotion so entire that a man would put his hand under another's feet to serve him. Ellicott notes that this exact construction occurs nowhere else and looks different from the familiar giving of the hand in token of good faith or submission, so that some ancient mode of doing homage may be meant; he records the Latin translator expanding it into two acts, giving the hand and being made subject. Delitzsch rejects the oath derivation outright, denying that the sense of submitting comes from any custom of clasping hands in swearing.

Ellicott and Delitzsch both read the whole sentence as glancing at the recent attempt on the throne, since it specifies that the king's sons submitted as well as the grandees; Ellicott is careful to distinguish the two groups, the princes being the officers listed earlier and not members of the royal house. Henry makes the same observation the occasion of his sharpest remark, that the brothers whose seniority gave them the prior title submitted anyway, because God both made this son king and made him fit to be one, and inclined their hearts so that the reign should be peaceable from the first. He sets the contrast with the father plainly: a better man came to the crown with much difficulty, after long delay and by slow steps, having more faith and so having it more tried.

On the greatness conferred, the interest is arithmetical as well as theological. Gill takes the magnifying to lie in the large share of wisdom and understanding given for governing. Ellicott renders the clause literally, that a glory of kingship was put upon him such as had not come upon any king over Israel before, and observes that only two predecessors existed, or three if Ishbosheth is counted. Delitzsch reaches the same conclusion by grammar, holding that the construction means simply none and implies no more than that there had been more than one, namely Saul, Ishbosheth and David, whose own reign he grants had been covered with glory. Henry, less cautious, thinks the man's very countenance and presence must have had something awful in them, and that none of the judges or kings before him made such a figure or lived in such splendour.
26:
Wesley explains the seam. Having mentioned the anointing, the writer described how the heir was actually settled in his kingdom, and now returns to his main business, bringing the old king to the end of his day, leaving him asleep and drawing the curtains about him. Ellicott makes the same point grammatically, preferring the pluperfect, David had reigned, and both he and Delitzsch read the phrase over all Israel as pointing back to the earlier period when only Judah acknowledged him. Gill calls the reign long and glorious and leaves it there.

On the length both of the close readers correct the round figure. Delitzsch and Ellicott note that the seven years at Hebron were more exactly seven and a half, and Ellicott adds that the verse is a duplicate of the notice in Kings with two words dropped. Henry observes that forty years was the term of Moses, of several judges, of Saul before him and of Solomon after.

The obituary formula draws out the most feeling. Clarke breaks it into four and dwells on each: an age long enough that living further could not be desired, days full in the sense of seeing everything he had lived for accomplished or well forward, riches attested by the sums left for the temple, and honour beyond any crowned head before or since. Ellicott prefers the literal satisfied with days, the sense the Greek and Latin took, and quotes the Syriac reading. Wesley makes satisfied the point of the whole: the man had enough of this world and knew when he had enough, and was very willing to go to a better. Henry says it both ways, loaded with these things and also satiated with them, noting that a soldier from his youth was preserved through every danger of a military life and died in his bed, yet in the bed of honour; a good man, he adds, will soon be full of days and riches but never satisfied with them, there being no satisfaction except in the loving kindness of God. Gill supplies the age, seventy.

Where the fuller story was to be found produces the one real division. Henry has the registers begun by Samuel in his lifetime and continued after his death by Nathan and Gad, and says flatly that they were then in being but are now lost, drawing the lesson that good use may be made of church histories which are authentic without being inspired. Clarke agrees they are lost, except for what survives scattered in the later books, and insists on the corollary that none of the books we now possess are the records here cited. Wesley locates them instead in the chronicles of the kingdom, kept by Nathan and Gad as historiographers and not merely as prophets, out of which they or others afterwards selected under divine direction what would serve the church in later ages. Ellicott stays with the words themselves, since the Hebrew term means a matter or transaction as readily as a word, so that Gesenius could render the phrase as a book entitled The Acts of Samuel; Delitzsch refers the question to his introduction. Delitzsch, Ellicott and Wesley all gloss the times that went over him as the vicissitudes of fortune, good and evil, and identify the kingdoms of the countries as the neighbours with whom Israel had dealings, Philistia, Edom, Moab, Ammon and Aram.

Two witnesses will not end on a formula. Clarke quotes Delaney's summary, a peasant by birth and a prince by merit, hero in youth, monarch in manhood and saint in age, and calls the matter of Uriah the great and only blot, adding that no man ever suffered more for a sin nor repented more deeply. Henry, surprised that so illustrious a close should follow the second book of Samuel, makes the same connection: the repentance was as remarkable as the offence.
